lines.en: Hi Omar! Our last day of C1. How does it feel?
Strange. It feels like a goodbye and a beginning at the same time.
What she did not say in the meeting spoke far louder than anything she actually said.
It is one thing to say you agree, and quite another to mean it.
Not until you compare the two versions of the story do you notice how carefully the facts were arranged.
Little did the audience realize that his praise was, in fact, the sharpest criticism of all.
And how is your formal reply to your manager doing? Still in draft?
However brilliant your idea may be, presenting it in the wrong register can kill it before anyone listens.
Not until you have written the same message in three different styles do you understand what register really means.
Admittedly, 'give us a ring' sounds friendlier than 'contact us', but no company report would ever use it.
Rarely does a speaker notice how often they shift register, yet listeners judge them on it every time.
I rewrote it nine times. Each version is more careful than the last.
What cautious writers understand is that a well-placed 'perhaps' can be more persuasive than a bold claim.
It is generally accepted that stress affects memory, but the strength of that effect is still debated.
Not until every alternative explanation has been ruled out should we call the theory proven.
Rarely can a single study settle a scientific question, whatever the headlines may claim.
Careful, but not boring, I hope. Did you keep the idiom?
What makes idioms so difficult is that their meaning rarely has anything to do with their words.
It is no use crying over spilled milk; what matters now is how we fix the situation.
Not until he was offered the job did he realize he had been sitting on the fence for months.
Rarely does anyone hit the nail on the head as precisely as she did in that discussion.
The manager will probably disagree with me anyway.
What distinguishes a strong argument from a loud one is the quality of its evidence, not its volume.
Admittedly, your plan has its strengths; nevertheless, it ignores the single most important risk.
Not until both sides agree on the facts can any real debate about solutions begin.
Rarely does anyone win a debate by shouting; more often, they simply lose the audience.
You sound like a researcher defending a paper now.
What the data demonstrate is not that the method fails, but that its success depends on conditions we rarely meet.
It is essential that every participant be informed of the risks before the experiment begins.
Not until the experiment had been repeated forty times did the journal agree to publish the results.
What remains unclear is whether the effect exists outside the laboratory.
If the paper gets rejected, I will call it 'not entirely successful'.
Calling the hurricane 'a bit of wind' is the kind of understatement the British have turned into an art.
What the reviewer called 'not entirely successful' was, by any honest measure, a complete disaster.
It would be an understatement to say the guests were surprised; several of them are still talking about it.
Rarely has 'we need to talk' preceded good news.
You always hide the point in the middle. Put it up front.
It was not the storm that destroyed the harvest, but the drought that had come before it.
What the report actually says, contrary to the headlines, is that more research is needed.
All I ask is that you listen before you judge.
What we need is not more information but the courage to act on what we already know.
And I must choose every word carefully this time.
What the law forbids and what the law punishes are two very different things.
It is one thing to hear the words, another to listen to them, and quite another to understand them.
However similar 'remember' and 'remind' may look, confusing them can change a message completely.
What a dictionary gives you is the skeleton of a word; its flesh and blood come from use.
When this is over, you should write your story. All of it.
What every good storyteller knows is that the ending must feel both surprising and inevitable.
It is not the events themselves that make a story, but the order in which they are revealed.
Not until the final chapter do we learn that the narrator has been lying to us all along.
Rarely does the first version of a story survive; the best ones are told and retold until they shine.
My story has too many unknowns, like bad science.
What separates science from opinion is the willingness to say 'we do not know yet'.
However elegant a theory may be, nature has no obligation to be elegant.
Not until we admit the limits of our knowledge does real learning begin.
Rarely is 'the science says' the end of a conversation; it should be the beginning of a better one.
Unknowns are fine. They are the beginning of every big question.
What makes a question philosophical is not that it has no answer, but that every answer opens ten more.
Not until we face the possibility that we are wrong do we truly begin to think.
It is argued that we do not see the world as it is, but as we are.
Rarely does philosophy give us answers; what it gives us are better questions.
My sister says I never talk about feelings, only ideas.
What empathy requires is not that we feel the same pain, but that we believe it is real.
Not until someone has sat with us in silence, without advice, do we feel truly heard.
It is said that courage is not the absence of fear, but the decision that something else matters more.
Little do we know of the storms inside the people we pass every day.
Feelings are also culture, you know.
What we call 'normal' is usually nothing more than the habits of the people we grew up around.
However global the world becomes, people still dream in the language of their childhood.
Not until you live abroad do you discover which parts of you are you, and which are your country.
What the immigrant packs last and never unpacks is a way of being polite.
And apparently everything else is media bias now.
What a headline chooses to shout and what it chooses to whisper tell you more than the story itself.
However neutral a report may sound, the choice of which expert to interview is already an opinion.
It is said that the camera never lies, but it certainly chooses where to look.
Rarely does a correction travel as far or as fast as the mistake it corrects.
You should write about that too. Public life needs honest writers.
What a society argues about in public tells you what it values in private.
However unpopular a truth may be, a healthy society must make room for it to be said.
What the crowd demands today, it may punish tomorrow; that is why leadership means more than listening.
Rarely does power give up its privileges voluntarily; every right we have was argued for, at length.
First I need to survive my own office.
What distinguishes a professional email from a casual one is not length, but the clarity of what happens next.
It is better to deliver bad news plainly and early than to wrap it in hopeful language until it is too late.
Were every meeting to end with a decision and a name, half the meetings would disappear.
Rarely has anyone been promoted for a beautifully formatted spreadsheet alone.
Survival needs jokes.
It is said that a pun is the lowest form of wit, usually by people who cannot make one.
However old a joke may be, it is new to anyone hearing it for the first time.
Not until you explain a joke do you realize how much of it lived in the timing.
Rarely does a meeting need less laughter, whatever the agenda claims.
And memories. My grandfather called yesterday.
What we remember is rarely what happened; it is the story we have told ourselves about what happened.
It is unsettling to realize that every time we recall a memory, we rewrite it a little.
The smell of jasmine, for no reason he could name, returned him to his grandmother's balcony.
Rarely do two siblings remember the same childhood.
What did he predict for your future this time?
What makes the future so hard to predict is not that it is hidden, but that it has not decided yet.
It is said that the best way to predict the future is to invent it.
However precise the forecast, the future retains the right to surprise us.
Rarely has the future arrived on schedule; it tends to come early, late, or dressed as something else.
He said freedom is doing the work nobody asked you to do.
What freedom means, if it means anything at all, is the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.
However wide our freedom, it ends where another person's freedom begins.
Not until we accept responsibility for our choices do those choices truly become ours.
Rarely is responsibility welcomed; it is usually accepted, quietly, by those who can no longer avoid it.
Then write it all, Omar. Persuade us.
What the reader owes you is nothing; every sentence must earn the reading of the next.
It is not enough to be right; you must be read.
Not until you have written for a hostile reader have you truly written persuasively.
Rarely does shouting convince the reader; the quiet, well-built sentence does.
And when the critics attack, I will remember our lesson on conflict.
Were both sides to state the other's position fairly, half the argument would end on its own.
It is said that you do not make peace with your friends; you make it with your enemies.
The apology arrived fifty years late, which is to say, it arrived.
Rarely does the first offer end a conflict; it merely proves that ending it is possible.
So this is what success looks like, at the end of C1.
What we call success is often only the visible tip of ten years of invisible work.
It is not the achievement that changes a person, but the person they had to become to reach it.
What she built, in the end, was not the company she had dreamed of, but something the dream had never imagined.
Rarely is the summit the point; the climb is.
What happens now? Do we just stop?
C2 is next, Omar. Proficiency. The last mountain.
Then we had better start climbing. When do we begin?
We already have. See you at the summit.
